Baby & Child

Sunburn in babies and children: care, warning signs and prevention

Updated: November 4, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

A child may look comfortable outdoors and develop sore, hot skin hours later. Sunburn is ultraviolet damage, not simply a sign that the weather felt hot. Move your child out of the sun and assess their age, skin, feeding and behaviour before choosing home care. A baby’s sunburn deserves prompt professional advice even when the area looks small.

What sunburn can look and feel like

Skin may feel warm, tender or painful, with redness, swelling or later peeling. Severe injury can blister. Colour change can be less obvious on brown or black skin, so look beyond redness to discomfort and the child’s overall condition. Signs often develop several hours after exposure and can worsen over the first day; a normal-looking patch immediately after an outing does not rule out damage.

Ultraviolet A and B rays can harm skin and eyes. UVB is strongly associated with burning, while UVA contributes to ageing and other damage; protection should cover both. Babies and young children need particular protection, and darker skin is not immune. A rash or fever after an outing is not automatically sunburn, so seek advice when the cause is unclear.

Decide who needs medical help

Contact a clinician promptly for any sunburn in a baby, especially under 1 year. NHS guidance also recommends urgent advice for a young child with sunburn. For any age, seek prompt assessment for blisters, a large affected area, substantial swelling, severe or worsening pain, fever, chills, vomiting, headache or a child who seems unwell. Home comfort measures can begin while you arrange advice; they should not postpone it.

Call emergency services if your child is difficult to wake, confused, collapses, has a seizure or has serious breathing difficulty, especially after heat exposure. Move them to a cooler place, remove excess layers and follow the dispatcher’s cooling instructions. Do not wait for a particular temperature or a trial of pain medicine. A baby under 3 months with a temperature of 38°C or higher needs urgent medical assessment; do not assume the sun explains the fever.

Cool gently and make the skin comfortable

Go indoors or into reliable shade. A cool, damp cloth or a cool bath can ease soreness; keep the child supervised and avoid making them shiver or too cold. Do not put ice or ice packs directly on sunburn. Pat dry gently, avoid rubbing and choose soft, loose clothing that does not press on sore areas.

For intact, mildly burned skin, an unperfumed moisturiser may help. A suitable aloe-containing moisturiser can soothe but cannot undo UV damage; raw leaves, scented gels or a product that stings are poor choices. Stop an irritating product. Ask about suitable products for an infant, and use medicated creams or numbing preparations only if the child’s clinician recommends them.

Keep feeds and fluids appropriate for age

Offer usual breastfeeds more often if wanted, or correctly prepared formula to an alert baby who can feed normally. Do not dilute formula. Young infants should not be given large amounts of plain water in place of milk. Guidance about small additional water feeds for formula-fed babies under 6 months varies locally, so ask a child-health professional rather than improvising after a burn.

From around 6 months, small drinks of water can accompany complementary foods while breast milk or formula remains important; older children can drink water regularly. Poor feeding, fewer wet nappies or less urine, dry mouth, unusual sleepiness or repeated vomiting need prompt advice. Fluids at home do not replace assessment of a sick or dehydrated baby.

Check pain medicines before giving them

Paracetamol, also called acetaminophen, may be appropriate, but it is not automatically suitable at every infant age or dose. For a baby with sunburn, ask the clinician what to use. US paediatric advice recommends professional guidance before acetaminophen under 2 years; product and age rules differ between countries. Use the child’s weight, the exact product strength and the advised dose, measured with an oral syringe rather than a kitchen spoon.

Ibuprofen has age and health restrictions: US guidance says not under 6 months unless a doctor directs it, while some UK products allow younger infants under specified conditions. Do not choose it for a dehydrated child, and check other illnesses or medicines with a pharmacist. Do not give aspirin for a child’s sunburn, double up ingredients or alternate pain medicines without advice. Severe pain despite appropriate relief needs reassessment.

Protect blisters and follow healing

Do not burst blisters, peel loose skin or scrub the burn. Blistering in a baby or child needs advice about assessment and protection. Recommendations about ointments can differ for intact sunburn and an open blister; use the clinician’s wound-care plan rather than putting petroleum jelly, antibiotics or several household remedies over the whole burn. Do not apply sunscreen into an open wound as a substitute for covering and care.

Increasing warmth or swelling, spreading redness, worsening pain, pus or fever can signal a complication and need review. Many mild burns settle over several days, often around a week, but there is no guaranteed healing date. Keep injured skin out of direct sun until healed. If it is not improving or you are unsure whether it is sunburn, seek assessment.

Understand the longer-term risk without blame

Repeated UV exposure and childhood sunburn increase later skin-cancer risk, including melanoma, and can contribute to premature skin ageing. A past burn does not mean a child will develop cancer. A fixed claim that every blistering burn doubles an individual’s risk, or that sunscreen removes a set percentage of all cancer risk, cannot predict what happens to your child.

Protection still matters after a mistake. Make the next outing easier with shade, suitable clothing and the right product available. Some medicines and medical conditions increase sun sensitivity; ask the prescriber or pharmacist when relevant without stopping treatment yourself. Sunscreen supports prevention but does not erase existing damage or make unlimited time in the sun safe.

Plan shade and clothing before sunscreen

Check the local UV index and heat advice, not only the temperature or whether the sky is blue. UV can be strong through cloud and can reflect from sand, water and snow. Limit exposure around the strongest part of the day; clock times vary with location and season. Babies under 6 months should stay out of direct sun, and older children also need shade and breaks.

Use loose, comfortable clothing with good coverage and a tight weave, or clothing labelled with a UV protection factor (UPF). A thin white shirt or ordinary swimsuit is not a guarantee of protection. Choose a broad-brimmed hat or neck-flap hat and well-fitting sunglasses with strong UVA and UVB protection. Avoid overheating: use a proper stroller canopy or shade, never a blanket draped over the pram, and check the child regularly.

Choose sunscreen with the baby’s age in mind

For children from 6 months, choose a broad-spectrum, water-resistant sunscreen with SPF 30 or higher, appropriate for the child and local label. SPF mainly describes protection from sunburn; the broad-spectrum claim adds UVA protection. Zinc oxide or titanium dioxide products may be less irritating for sensitive skin. A label saying “baby” does not itself prove that every formulation suits every child.

For babies under 6 months, shade and clothing come first. FDA advice is to ask a doctor before using sunscreen; the American Academy of Pediatrics allows a small amount on small exposed areas when adequate clothing and shade are unavailable. This is not permission for whole-body application followed by prolonged sun exposure. Ask about the situation and product rather than believing either that all sunscreen is harmless or that sunscreen chemicals are always more dangerous than sunlight.

Apply it well and reapply during the outing

Follow the label, generally applying before going outside and covering exposed areas evenly, including ears, neck and tops of feet. Keep sunscreen away from eyes and mouth. A lotion or cream is easier to control around a young child than a spray that could be inhaled; never spray directly onto the face. Check expiry and storage instructions, and stop a product that causes a rash or irritation.

Reapply at least every 2 hours outdoors and after swimming, sweating or towelling, following the product’s water-resistance instructions. A 40- or 80-minute water-resistant label does not mean waterproof or all-day protection. Clothing does not remove the need to protect skin left uncovered, and sunscreen does not replace shade. Share the plan with everyone caring for the child and arrange an earlier return indoors if protection is difficult.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Record the child’s age, exposure, skin changes, temperature, feeds and medicines used when asking for advice.

Agree on suitable cooling, skin care and pain relief, and know which changes need urgent help.

Prepare shade, protective clothes and an age-appropriate sunscreen plan before the next outing.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help organise exposure notes, symptoms, feeds, products and questions for the child’s clinician. It cannot grade a burn, diagnose heatstroke or infection, choose a medicine dose or decide that a baby is safe to treat at home.

When to seek help

Seek prompt clinical advice for a baby or young child with sunburn, or for blisters, extensive injury, worsening pain, poor feeding or illness. Call emergency services for difficulty waking, confusion, collapse, seizures or serious breathing difficulty. A baby under 3 months with a temperature of 38°C or higher needs urgent medical assessment.

Evidence notes updated: November 4, 2026

Key takeaways

  • A baby’s sunburn needs prompt professional advice; blisters or an unwell child need assessment.
  • Cool gently, avoid ice and blister manipulation, and keep injured skin out of direct sun.
  • Use age-appropriate milk feeds, fluids and pain medicines; never dilute formula.
  • Shade, clothing, hats and UV-protective glasses work alongside sunscreen.
  • Choose broad-spectrum SPF 30 or higher from 6 months and follow label and infant-specific advice.

Frequently asked questions

When is a child’s sunburn urgent?

Get prompt advice for a baby or young child, and for blisters, extensive injury, severe pain or illness at any age. Difficulty waking, confusion, collapse, seizures or serious breathing difficulty require emergency help. A fever of 38°C or higher under 3 months needs urgent assessment, whatever the apparent cause.

What can I put on the burned skin?

For intact, mild sunburn, a gentle unperfumed moisturiser may soothe after cooling. Ask about infant products and blister care. Avoid irritating home remedies and use medicated creams only on professional advice; a lotion cannot reverse UV damage.

How can I ease the pain?

Use a cool damp cloth or cool bath without chilling the child, soft clothing and suitable pain relief advised for their age and weight. Do not use ice. A baby should be assessed rather than given an assumed safe dose, and severe persistent pain needs review.

Which sunscreen and how often?

From 6 months, use a suitable broad-spectrum, water-resistant SPF 30 or higher. Follow the label, reapply at least every 2 hours outdoors and after water, sweat or towelling. Under 6 months, prioritise shade and clothing and ask about limited exposed-area use.

Can a baby burn on a cloudy or cool day?

Yes. UV is different from heat, can pass through clouds and reflects off nearby surfaces. Check local UV advice and protect the child even when the air feels comfortable.

Should I give a young baby extra water?

Continue breast milk or correctly prepared formula and seek advice if feeding or wet nappies decrease. Do not dilute formula or replace feeds with water. Guidance on small extra water feeds under 6 months varies locally, so ask a professional.

Should I pop a blister or peel the skin?

No. Leave it alone and obtain advice for a child’s blisters. A clinician can decide whether a dressing or treatment is needed. Seek review for worsening pain, swelling, spreading redness, pus or fever.

Does one burn mean future skin cancer?

No. Sunburn raises risk rather than predicting an individual outcome. Preventing further UV injury is worthwhile, without promising that sunscreen completely removes risk or blaming the family for a past mistake.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
